passage_text: Researchers studied the effect of three different auditory stimuli on participants’ reaction times during a simple visual detection task. The study recruited 90 healthy adults aged 18–35, randomly assigned to one of three groups: Control (no auditory stimulus), Treatment A (high‑frequency tone), and Treatment B (low‑frequency tone). Each participant completed 60 trials, and the mean reaction time (RT) and standard deviation (SD) were recorded for each group. The Control group had a mean RT of 350 ms (SD = 45 ms), Treatment A had a mean RT of 310 ms (SD = 38 ms), and Treatment B had a mean RT of 320 ms (SD = 42 ms). The researchers reported that both auditory stimuli reduced mean RT compared to the Control, with Treatment A showing the greatest improvement. The data were analyzed using one‑way ANOVA followed by post‑hoc Tukey tests. The study concluded that high‑frequency tones may facilitate faster visual processing in healthy adults.
stem: Which group had the lowest mean reaction time?

options.D: All groups had the same mean RT

explanation: The table shows Treatment A’s mean RT of 310 ms, which is lower than Control’s 350 ms and Treatment B’s 320 ms.
trap: Students may incorrectly assume the Control group has the lowest RT because it is the baseline.

stem: Which of the following would be the most appropriate control condition for this experiment?

options.A: A group exposed to a high‑frequency tone only
options.B: A group exposed to a low‑frequency tone only
options.C: A group exposed to no auditory stimulus
options.D: A group exposed to both high‑ and low‑frequency tones simultaneously

explanation: The Control group with no auditory stimulus serves as the baseline against which the effects of the tones are measured.
trap: Students may think the best control is the group with the least effect (e.g., low‑frequency tone) instead of no stimulus.

stem: Calculate the pooled standard deviation for the three groups.
explanation: With equal n = 30, pooled SD = sqrt((45² + 38² + 42²)/3) = sqrt(1744.3) = 41.8 ms.
trap: Students may incorrectly sum the SDs instead of using the variance formula.

stem: Which statistical test is least appropriate for comparing the mean RTs across the three groups?

options.B: Independent samples t‑test between Control and Treatment A
options.C: Paired t‑test between Control and Treatment B

explanation: A paired t‑test assumes the same participants are measured in both conditions, which is not the case here (independent groups).
trap: Students may think any t‑test is fine, overlooking the independence assumption.

stem: What is the percent reduction in mean reaction time for Treatment A relative to the Control group?
explanation: Correct: (350 - 310) / 350 x 100 = 11.4%. Why the others are wrong: B) 12.9% divides the 40 ms difference by Treatment A's mean (310) rather than the Control reference. C) 8.6% is the Treatment B reduction, (350 - 320) / 350. D) 40% reports the 40 ms difference as a percent.
trap: Students divide the 40 ms difference by the treated mean (310) instead of the Control baseline (350), or report 40 ms as 40%.
